extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of media and communication, journalism researchers, and readers interested in history of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly chapter-level analysis of Walter Lippmann’s account of how news is created, circulated, and rhetorically shaped (stereotypes, symbols, myths) and how these processes construct mass consensus and influence public opinion. It situates Lippmann in the post‑WWI political/technological context (newspapers, radio, reproducible content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques of creation and news sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Lippmann’s Public Opinion focuses on the techniques of creation and news sharing soon after the conclusion of World War I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news by examining the concrete techniques through which news items are produced and circulated in their historical-political context (e.g., post‑WWI settlement, Treaty of Versailles, Wilson’s Fourteen Points). Consider how those techniques shape what becomes ‘news’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of media/technological forms (newspapers, radio, reproducible contents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The social impact of newspapers, along with the diffusion of radio and reproducible contents, reveals rapid functional shifts of public opinion within urban areas and a transformation of collective information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing news, account for medium effects — how the form (print, radio, reproducible media) enables different circulation patterns and alters collective information. Pay attention to technological change as a driver of shifts in public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to stereotypes, symbols and myths as formative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes, symbols and myths were not to be underestimated in the years that herald the growth of totalitarianism, especially if referred to propaganda techniques and informative persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically inspect news content for embedded stereotypes, nationalistic symbols, and popular myths. Treat these cultural elements as mechanisms by which persuasive or propagandistic discourse operates; their presence is a substantive signal about how audience attitudes may be manufactured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of rhetorical patterns in journalistic discourse (construction of mass consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The construction of mass consensus depends on the rhetorical patterns inspiring the journalistic discourse," as Lippmann underlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the rhetorical structures and devices journalists and press agents use (framing, metaphor, narrative patterns). Use rhetorical analysis to trace how consensus is rhetorically engineered rather than assuming it emerges spontaneously from facts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of stereotypes influencing public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter stresses the need to probe the “nature of news” and foster “the detection of stereotypes” influencing public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit, methodical efforts to identify and unpack stereotypes within news texts as part of evaluating their social effect. Detection here is both analytical (identifying instances) and normative (assessing their impact on public opinion formation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate analysis of the social impact of reporters and press agents
rubrics_metrics.description: An "accurate analysis of the social impact of reporters and press agents" is recommended, particularly ahead of later media 'fallout' (electrification and beyond).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not only content but the social role and practices of reporting actors (reporters, press agents) — their institutional positions, routines, and influence — when judging the significance and effects of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probe the 'nature of news' historically and socially
rubrics_metrics.description: The work recommends probing the 'nature of news' in order to understand transformations of collective information and the rhetorical roots of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt historically informed and socially grounded inquiry into what counts as news, how news norms evolve, and how those norms interact with broader political and cultural forces; avoid ahistorical or purely formalist evaluations.
